It is becoming f*cking dangerous: Microsoft Research made Claude Code 23.6% cheaper by letting it learn from its own past sessions, and 6 more repos stop it from repeating your old mistakes

1. Install TokenEconomizer and let it learn your repo from past sessions, a fact loads at session start once 3 sessions confirm it, and contradicted facts get dropped: https://github.com/microsoft/TokenEconomizer

2. Run loom, ClickHouse's self-hosted MCP server, so what one agent learns the next one can find, its Claude Code plugin loads context at start and records each session: https://github.com/ClickHouse/loom

3. Run npx @globalmpc/nomore to find the instructions you repeated in 2+ sessions and turn them into CLAUDE.md rules that survive compaction: https://github.com/globalmpc/nomore

4. Add stalemap to catch dependencies that changed after the model's training cutoff, it writes a ranked list of changes into CLAUDE.md before the agent starts: https://github.com/Umair/stalemap

5. Install landmines to find open GitHub issues filed against the exact versions in your lockfile, the agent's edit stops once and gets the workaround from the thread: https://github.com/devanshranjan10/landmines

6. Open Rulebook to see every CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md across your projects, it flags diverged files, broken @imports and files over 200 lines: https://github.com/disinfeqt/rulebook

7. Give small jobs to lean agents, subagents that start at about 7.4k tokens instead of 131.1k because they skip CLAUDE.md, the skills list and MCP tools: https://github.com/mdalexandre/claude-code-lean-agents

TokenEconomizer on 277 SWE-Bench tasks: 18.4% to 30.9% lower cost across 5 setups, cheaper in all 30 cells

All 7 repos are less than 6 weeks old, Rulebook needs macOS 14+

your AI coding agent keeps making the same mistakes because it forgets what it learned in previous sessions.

these 7 GitHub projects are designed to fix that.

they help Claude Code remember project knowledge, reuse past solutions, detect outdated dependencies, find known bugs, and stop wasting tokens repeating work.

here’s what each one does:

1. TokenEconomizer : make your agent learn from experience

Microsoft Research’s plugin learns useful facts from completed coding sessions and brings them into future sessions. it also reduces unused tools and intervenes when the agent gets stuck.

https://github.com/microsoft/TokenEconomizer

2. Loom : shared memory between agents

ClickHouse’s self-hosted MCP server gives agents shared long-term memory, document search, and code intelligence, so one agent’s discoveries can help the next.

https://github.com/ClickHouse/loom

3. NoMore : stop repeating instructions

finds instructions you’ve repeated across multiple sessions and turns the ones you approve into persistent CLAUDE.md rules.

https://github.com/globalmpc/nomore

4. Stalemap : catch outdated dependencies

checks which dependencies changed after the model’s training cutoff and gives your coding agent updated API and changelog context before it starts.

https://github.com/Umair/stalemap

5. Landmines : find known dependency problems

checks your project’s locked dependency versions against open GitHub issues, helping your agent find known bugs and existing workarounds.

6. Rulebook : audit your agent instructions

a native macOS app that scans CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md files across projects, identifies diverged files, broken imports, and oversized instruction files.

https://github.com/disinfeqt/rulebook

7. Lean Agents : reduce subagent overhead

two lightweight Claude Code subagents that start at roughly 7.4K tokens instead of 131.1K by skipping unnecessary instructions, skills, and MCP tools.

https://github.com/mdalexandre/claude-code-lean-agents

the TokenEconomizer benchmark is particularly interesting:

across 277 SWE-Bench tasks, it reported 18.4%–30.9% lower costs across five agent-model setups, with lower costs in all 30 repository-combination cells.

one important detail: Rulebook requires macOS 14 or later.

the bigger idea is simple: stop making your AI agent learn the same lessons from scratch every time you start a session.

give your agents memory, better context, and fewer opportunities to repeat old mistakes.

Google just dropped a nine-page paper on Harness Engineering, and it changes everything about how we build autonomous agents

The core formula is simple:

Agent = Model + Harness

In other words, an AI model on its own is not an agent. What turns it into a reliable force for getting work done is the infrastructure we build around it

But what does this infrastructure consist of?

1. Guides: Rules and instructions that turn lessons from past failures into lasting knowledge

2. Sensors: Tests, linters, and validation tools that prevent any incorrect output from moving to the next stage

3. Agentic Loop: A cycle of planning, execution, review, and correction, with budget limits and the option to escalate to a human

4. External Memory: Memory outside the model for preserving decisions, project state, and the outcomes of previous sessions

5. Permissions: Control over the agent's access to tools and the boundaries of its autonomy

6. Observability: Logging and monitoring of all activities, costs, errors, and retries

But the story doesn't end here!

A few open-source projects to get hands-on with this field:

→Google Harness
→Learn Harness Engineering
→Awesome Agent Harness
→Harness Engineering

And now, a more intriguing concept:

Graph Engineering

Imagine having several independent agents, each with its own Harness

One does research, another analyzes, a third writes code, and a fourth validates the output

Now, if one fails, its failure can become a signal for improving the performance of the others

At this point, we're no longer dealing with a chatbot or a simple agent, we're looking at a multi-agent execution system

One thing we shouldn't forget:

Hermes can be thought of as the agent's execution environment, a place where tools, skills, memory, and workflows come together.

Harness Engineering helps make this environment controllable, measurable, and reliable

I think the future doesn't belong to those who simply choose a more powerful model, it belongs to those who build a better system around the model

The model is the brain, the Harness is the execution system, and the Graph is the network of brains working together
